The Act of October 27, 1972 (86 Stat. 1299; 16 U.S.C. 460bb) is amended as follows:

    (1) in subsection 2(a), at the end thereof, add the following: “For the purposes of this Act, the southern end of the town of Marshall shall be considered to be the Marshall Boat Works. The following additional lands are also hereby included within the boundaries of the recreation area: Marin County Assessor’s parcel numbered 119–040–04, 119–040–05, 119–040–18, 166–202–03, 166–010–06, 166–010–07, 166–010–24, 166–010–25, 119–240–19, 166–010–10, 166–010–22, 119–240–03, 119–240–51, 119–240–52, 119–240–54, 166–010–12, 166–010–13, and 119–235–10.”.
 
    (2) in subsection 5(b), change “three” to “five” and add at the end thereof: “Provided, That the terms of those members who have been either appointed or reappointed subsequent to January 1, 1979, shall be extended so as to expire not before June 1, 1985.”; and
 
    (3) 
in subsection 5(g), change “ten” to “twenty”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is only a technical amendment adjusting boundaries and numbers, with no outside party named. But section 5 of the amended Act (16 U.S.C. 460bb-4) is, from background knowledge rather than the text itself, the Golden Gate National Recreation Area Advisory Commission, a body of non-federal members that advises the Secretary. Lengthening members' terms from three to five years and the commission's life from ten to twenty years continues that outside advisory participation. Confidence is moderate because the section never says on its face who the members are.
fable.s: the terms of those members who have been either appointed or reappointed subsequent to January 1, 1979, shall be extended so as to expire not before June 1, 1985

opus.w: Section 5 of the 1972 Golden Gate National Recreation Area Act sets up the Advisory Commission, whose non-federal members advise the Secretary of the Interior on managing the area. This amendment lengthens members' terms and extends the commission's existence, keeping that outside advisory input in place. The tempting reading is that this is only a boundary and housekeeping change. That fails because the amended provisions govern an advisory commission of non-federal members, even though the commission is not named in the amendment itself.
opus.s: in subsection 5(b), change “three” to “five” and add at the end thereof: “Provided, That the terms of those members who have been either appointed or reappointed subsequent to January 1, 1979, shall be extended so as to expire not before June 1, 1985.”
opus.b:
I'm labelling this **Yes**, with moderate confidence (about 0.6).

1. **The tempting reading and why it fails.** At first glance this looks like a pure boundary and housekeeping amendment, with nothing about outsiders taking part in decisions. But the Act being amended (16 U.S.C. 460bb, the 1972 law creating the Golden Gate National Recreation Area) uses section 5 to set up the area's Advisory Commission. That commission is made up of members appointed from outside the federal government, and it advises the Secretary of the Interior on how the area is managed and developed. Paragraph (2) lengthens members' terms from three to five years, and paragraph (3), going by the statute's structure, extends the commission's lifespan from ten to twenty years. So the amendment keeps an advisory body of non-federal members in place to advise on federal decisions.

2. **Why the confidence is only moderate.** The amendment never names the commission or says who its members are. The Yes label depends on outside knowledge of what subsection 5 covers, so the evidence is indirect. Examples 10 and 12 suggest that this kind of uncertainty about an advisory body should still lean toward Yes.

qwen_chat.w: This section primarily amends the boundaries of a recreation area by adding specific land parcels. While it also adjusts the terms of members of a commission, it does not explicitly require consultation with outside parties, public comment, or define the commission's membership as including non-federal entities in this text. The adjustment of term lengths is an administrative change to an existing body, not a mechanism for public participation in a decision. Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: The Act of October 27, 1972 (86 Stat. 1299; 16 U.S.C. 460bb) is amended as follows: (1) in subsection 2(a), at the end thereof, add the following: “For the purposes of this Act, the southern end of the town of Marshall shall be considered to be the Marshall Boat Works. The following additional lands are also hereby included within the boundaries of the recreation area: Marin County Assessor’s parcel numbered 119–040–04, 119–040–05, 119–040–18, 166–202–03, 166–010–06, 166–010–07, 166–010–24, 166–010–25, 119–240–19, 166–010–10, 166–010–22, 119–240–03, 119–240–51, 119–240–52, 119–240–54, 166–010–12, 166–010–13, and 119–235–10.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section amends provisions regarding the terms of members of a commission (subsection 5(b)), it implies the existence of an advisory body with outside members, thus constituting participation. However, the text itself only adjusts numerical values (term lengths, number of members) and does not explicitly describe the composition of the board or require consultation with outside parties. More importantly, the primary content of the section is the expansion of land boundaries for a recreation area. Without explicit language requiring consultation, public comment, or defining the board as having non-federal members in this specific text, it is safer to classify this as "No" based on the lack of direct participation mechanisms described. The definition requires that the section *involve* participation. Merely adjusting the term of office for a board whose composition isn't detailed here doesn't inherently demonstrate the *process* of participation (consultation/coordination) with outsiders. The section is primarily about land boundaries and administrative term adjustments.
